newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-A.H. Belo bets on broadcasting with new deal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-A.H. Belo bets on broadcasting with new deal.

text.p: A.H. Belo Corp, owner of the Dallas Morning News, is betting its future on broadcasting by buying out Providence Journal Co and is well-placed to make the strategic shift work, analysts said.

While its stock dropped 3-3/8 to 34-1/8 on news that the $1.5 billion deal would batter Belo's 1997 earnings per share, industry analysts liked Belo's aggressive commitment to the higher-value broadcast business.
Under the deal announced on Thursday, Belo's share of cash flow from broadcasting will jump from 45 to 60 percent.
"I think you'll see more growth in television," said Dennis McAlpine of Goldman Sachs, adding that Belo has already shown itself a strong station manager in recent years.
"They feel they've demonstrated to themselves as well as the outside world that they can run TV stations well. To that extent, I think it's an opportunistic acquisition," he said.

Belo's shares came under pressure because of a widespread perception that it had been on the generous side and because company officials said the acquisition would dilute earnings per share by 50 percent or more in 1997. The dilution on cash flow in 1997 would be about 20 percent, they said.
But few in the market had any argument with the strategic move further towards broadcasting.

"Belo has an extremely attractive newspaper in Dallas, which is better than average, but broadcasting is still considered to be an industry of superior growth and superior returns," said Kara Cheseby of Legg Mason Wood Walker.

Belo is not the first publisher to chart such a route. Tribune Co, the owner of the Chicago Tribune, earlier this year bought Renaissance Communications Corp for $1.13 billion and both Gannett Co Inc and the New York Times Co have also moved steadily into broadcasting.

The easing of regulatory limitations on station ownership and audience reach has spurred a flurry of acquisitions in both radio and television and many media groups have been anxious to act quickly or else get left behind.
Building up an attractive portfolio of stations allows owners far greater negotiating power in terms of network affiliation and programming.
Newspapers, even those with firm market pentration such as the Dallas Morning News and the Providence Journal-Bulletin, have meanwhile continued to see advertizing siphoned off by other media.
With the acquisition, Belo will become the eighth largest U.S. television group and its audience reach will grow from 8 percent now to 12.3 percent, the nation's tenth largest.

Most analysts agreed with Belo executives' assertions that Belo's seven existing network-affiliated stations -- three CBS, three ABC and one UPN -- make a strong geographic and network mix with Providence Journal's portfolio of five NBC affiliates, two Fox, one ABC and one CBS.
And Belo's commitment to the move was underlined by its decision to increase a planned buyback of 3.6 million shares up to 13.6 million.
"They are putting their money where their mouth is," said Charles Baker, an analyst with Salomon Brothers.
Baker and others said Belo has performed well with its existing stations. "Their competitors always tell you Belo is a tough competitor. They are really good at local news."

While the acquisition of Providence Journal's NBC affiliate in Seattle (KING-TV) was seen as the jewel in the crown of the deal, analysts were not as optimistic as Belo management about prospects for the Television Food Network and America's Health Network, which it will also pick up.
Both those operations are now cash-flow negative.
